title: PostgreSQL Isolation Levels Explained With Examples
description: PostgreSQL isolation levels explained: Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable, with two-session demos, real errors and retry rules.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: 13.4 Data Consistency Checks at the Application Level

reviewNotes: Regular Saturday article (not a series part). Topic from Google autocomplete: 'postgresql isolation levels', '... explained', '... default', '... serializable', 'postgresql repeatable read vs serializable', and 'postgresql could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. Not covered by any live article or earlier draft; Part 11 (MVCC) shows one Repeatable Read example and is linked rather than repeated. TEST ENVIRONMENT: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS with PostgreSQL 18.7 (18.7-1.pgdg24.04+5, official PGDG binaries). As in earlier runs, apt could not install postgresql-18 because its dependency liburing2 comes from archive.ubuntu.com, which the sandbox network blocks; I extracted the PGDG postgresql-18 / postgresql-client-18 .debs and ran initdb/pg_ctl/psql with a stub liburing (io_method=worker, the default). SQL behaviour and messages are those of the real 18.7 binaries. Every two-session demo was run with two concurrent psql sessions in the order printed, from the reset data; outputs are real (psql '(n rows)' footers kept, some echo lines trimmed, and the comments '-- Terminal 1, first SELECT' etc. in output blocks are labels I added). The pid 1407 in the pg_locks output is from the sandbox. Docs followed: PostgreSQL 18 documentation at /docs/18/ (postgresql.org/docs/current now shows version 19). EDITOR CHECKS: (1) The pg_hba default on Ubuntu is peer auth, so the article does not show logging in as report_user; it shows pg_db_role_setting instead and states the SHOW result (tested with trust auth in the sandbox). The 'role setting wins over database setting' claim was tested. (2) The retry loop is pseudocode, not a specific driver. (3) The PL/pgSQL remark (catching 40001 inside a function does not replace a client retry) is reasoning from the docs' 'retry the complete transaction' rule, not a doc quote.

data.text: PostgreSQL has three working transaction isolation levels: Read Committed (the default), Repeatable Read and Serializable. You can also ask for Read Uncommitted, but PostgreSQL quietly runs it as Read Committed, so dirty reads never happen. The level decides which committed changes from other sessions your transaction can see, and which conflicts PostgreSQL stops with an error.

In this tutorial you will run every level yourself with two psql sessions, watch a non-repeatable read, a lost update and a write skew happen, and see the exact errors PostgreSQL 18 raises: could not serialize access due to concurrent update and could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions. You will also learn how to set the level per transaction, per session, per user and per database, and why your application must retry on SQLSTATE 40001.
How PostgreSQL isolation levels work

Every transaction in PostgreSQL reads from a snapshot: a list of which transactions had committed when the snapshot was taken. Rows written by transactions outside the snapshot are invisible to you, even if they commit while you are reading. If you want the full picture of row versions, xmin and xmax, read PostgreSQL DBA Part 11: MVCC, xmin/xmax and Row Visibility.
The isolation level mainly decides when the snapshot is taken and what happens when two transactions touch the same data:

items.content: Read Committed takes a new snapshot at the start of every statement. Two SELECTs in one transaction can return different results.

Repeatable Read takes one snapshot at the first query or data-changing statement of the transaction (not at BEGIN) and keeps it until the end. If you try to update a row someone else changed and committed after your snapshot, PostgreSQL rolls you back.
Serializable works like Repeatable Read and also watches for read/write patterns that could not happen if the transactions ran one at a time. When it finds one, it cancels one transaction.

data.text: The SQL standard defines the levels by which phenomena (anomalies) they must prevent. A dirty read is reading another transaction's uncommitted data. A non-repeatable read is re-reading a row and finding it changed by a committed transaction. A phantom read is re-running a query with a WHERE condition and getting a different set of rows. A serialization anomaly is a result that no one-at-a-time order of the transactions could produce. This is how PostgreSQL behaves at each level, according to the PostgreSQL 18 documentation:

Two cells are stricter than the standard requires. Read Uncommitted never shows uncommitted data, because PostgreSQL maps it to Read Committed. Repeatable Read does not allow phantom reads, because the whole transaction uses one snapshot. The standard only sets minimum protections, so this is allowed.
Sample setup
Create a scratch database with two small tables: accounts for money transfers and doctors for an on-call rota. Run this as the postgres user (sudo -u postgres psql).

data.caption: Create the sample tables

data.text: The demos change data, so run this reset before each one to start from the same values:

data.caption: Reset the sample data between demos

data.text: Open two terminals and connect both with sudo -u postgres psql -d isodemo. In the code below, -- Terminal 1 and -- Terminal 2 tell you where to type each statement, in the order shown. Terminal 2 statements outside a BEGIN run in autocommit mode, so they commit straight away.
Check and set the isolation level
The current transaction's level is in the setting transaction_isolation. The default for new transactions is default_transaction_isolation:

data.code:
SHOW transaction_isolation;
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;
data.caption: Check the isolation level

data.code:
transaction_isolation
-----------------------
 read committed
(1 row)

 default_transaction_isolation
-------------------------------
 read committed
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: To change the level for one transaction, put it in BEGIN, or run SET TRANSACTION as the first statement after BEGIN. Both forms do the same thing:

data.caption: Two ways to set the level for one transaction

data.code:
transaction_isolation
-----------------------
 repeatable read
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The level cannot change once the transaction has run its first query or data-changing statement (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, FETCH or COPY). We will see the error for that in the common mistakes section. Ways to set a default for more than one transaction are covered near the end.
Read Committed: each statement sees fresh data
Non-repeatable read in action
Terminal 1 reads Asha's balance twice in one transaction. Between the two reads, Terminal 2 withdraws 1,000 and commits.

data.caption: Read Committed sees commits made between statements

data.code:
-- Terminal 1, first SELECT
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)

-- Terminal 2
UPDATE 1

-- Terminal 1, second SELECT
 balance
---------
 4000.00
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The same query in the same transaction returned two different values. That is a non-repeatable read. It is normal in Read Committed because the second SELECT took a new snapshot that includes Terminal 2's commit. Each single statement still sees a consistent picture; only the transaction as a whole does not.
Read Uncommitted does not show dirty data
Reset the data. Now Terminal 1 sets Asha's balance to 0 but does not commit, and Terminal 2 reads it at Read Uncommitted.

data.caption: Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed

data.code:
-- Terminal 2
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Terminal 2 still sees 5000.00. SHOW transaction_isolation would print read uncommitted, but the behaviour is Read Committed. You cannot get dirty reads in PostgreSQL at any level.
The lost update problem and three ways to fix it

A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value in the application, and the second write silently overwrites the first. It is the most common concurrency bug in Read Committed code.
The bug: read, compute in the app, write
Reset the data. Ravi has 3000. Two payments run at the same time: one withdraws 500, the other 800. Each reads the balance, subtracts in the application and writes the result back as a fixed number.

data.caption: Lost update in Read Committed

data.text: The correct balance is 1700 (3000 - 500 - 800). The 500 withdrawal was lost. Terminal 2's UPDATE waited for Terminal 1's row lock, then wrote its precomputed value on top of the committed one. PostgreSQL did nothing wrong: the value 2200 came from the application, based on an old read.
Fix 1: let the UPDATE do the arithmetic
Reset the data and run the same two payments, but write the change relative to the current value:

data.caption: Atomic update in Read Committed

data.text: This works because in Read Committed a waiting UPDATE does not use its old copy of the row. When the first transaction commits, PostgreSQL re-checks the WHERE clause against the newest version of the row and applies the change to that version. This is the simplest fix whenever the new value can be written as an expression.
Fix 2: lock the row first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
When the application really must read the value first (for example to check the balance is enough), lock the row while reading it. Reset the data and run:

data.caption: Pessimistic locking with FOR UPDATE

data.code:
-- Terminal 2, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE after Terminal 1 committed
 balance
---------
 2500.00
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Terminal 2 waited and then saw the committed 2500, so its calculation was correct. The cost is waiting, and if two transactions lock rows in a different order you can hit a deadlock; see PostgreSQL Deadlock Detected: Causes, Examples and Fixes.
Fix 3: use Repeatable Read and retry
The third fix is to raise the isolation level, so PostgreSQL detects the conflict for you. That is the next section.
Repeatable Read: one snapshot for the whole transaction
Reset the data. Repeat the first demo, but start Terminal 1 at Repeatable Read, and then let Terminal 1 try to update the row that Terminal 2 changed.

data.caption: Repeatable Read keeps the first snapshot

data.code:
-- first SELECT
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)

-- second SELECT, after Terminal 2 committed
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 200 WHERE account_id = 1;
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 4000.00
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Three things happened:

items.content: The second SELECT still showed 5000.00. The whole transaction reads from the snapshot taken at its first SELECT, so reports and multi-step calculations see stable data.

The UPDATE failed with could not serialize access due to concurrent update. A Repeatable Read transaction cannot modify or lock a row that another transaction changed and committed after its snapshot. Updating 5000 + 200 would have thrown away Terminal 2's withdrawal, so PostgreSQL refused.
After the error the transaction is aborted. Every further statement fails until you run ROLLBACK. After the rollback, a new snapshot shows the real value, 4000.00.

data.text: This error is how Repeatable Read prevents the lost update from the previous section. The right reaction is to roll back and run the whole transaction again; the second time it starts with a snapshot that already includes the other change. The error always has SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure). In psql you can print it right after the error:

data.code: \echo :LAST_ERROR_SQLSTATE
data.caption: Show the SQLSTATE of the last error in psql

data.text: Only transactions that change or lock rows can get this error. A read-only transaction at Repeatable Read never has serialization conflicts, which makes it a good, cheap choice for reports that run several queries and need them to agree.
Write skew: why Repeatable Read is not always enough
Repeatable Read stops two transactions from changing the same row. It does not stop two transactions that each read the same data and then change different rows. This anomaly is called write skew.
The rule in our hospital is: at least one doctor must stay on call. Dr. Rao and Dr. Iyer are on call. Both want to go off call at the same moment, and each checks the rule first.
Repeatable Read lets the rule break
Reset the data and run:

data.caption: Write skew under Repeatable Read

data.code:
doctor_name | on_call
-------------+---------
 Dr. Iyer    | f
 Dr. Khan    | f
 Dr. Rao     | f
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Both commits succeeded and nobody is on call. Each transaction was correct on its own, and they never touched the same row, so Repeatable Read saw no conflict. Run one after the other, the second would have seen a count of 1 and stopped.
Serializable catches it
Reset the data and run exactly the same steps with SERIALIZABLE. This time Terminal 2 also retries after the error:

data.caption: Serializable prevents write skew

data.code:
-- Terminal 1
COMMIT;
COMMIT

-- Terminal 2
COMMIT;
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.

-- Terminal 2, retry
 count
-------
     1
(1 row)

 doctor_name | on_call
-------------+---------
 Dr. Iyer    | t
 Dr. Khan    | f
 Dr. Rao     | f
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Terminal 1 committed. Terminal 2's COMMIT failed, and its UPDATE was rolled back. Notice that the error came at COMMIT, not at the UPDATE: with Serializable a failure can appear on any statement, including COMMIT, so the application must check the result of COMMIT too. On retry, Terminal 2 saw only one doctor on call, and the application logic kept Dr. Iyer on call. The rule holds.
How Serializable tracks reads: SIReadLock
To detect these patterns, PostgreSQL records what each serializable transaction has read using predicate locks. They appear in pg_locks with mode SIReadLock. Reset the data and run:

data.caption: See predicate locks in pg_locks

data.code:
pid  | locktype | relation | page |    mode
------+----------+----------+------+------------
 1407 | relation | doctors  |      | SIReadLock
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The count scanned the whole table with a sequential scan, so the predicate lock covers the whole doctors relation. With an index scan you would see smaller page or tuple locks instead. Your pid will differ.

These locks never block anyone and cannot cause deadlocks. They are only bookkeeping used to decide whether a transaction must be cancelled. Unlike row locks, they can stay in pg_locks for a while after the transaction commits, until overlapping read/write transactions finish.
Long reports: SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE

A long report running at Serializable has the usual tracking overhead and can, in rare cases, be cancelled. If you declare it SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE, PostgreSQL may wait at the start until it can take a snapshot that is guaranteed safe. After that the report runs without the serializable overhead and cannot be cancelled by a serialization failure. The documentation recommends this mode for long-running reports and backups.

data.caption: A safe read-only report transaction

data.code:
total_balance
---------------
      15500.00
(1 row)

 transaction_read_only
-----------------------
 on
(1 row)

ERROR:  cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction
data.caption: Output

data.text: READ ONLY also protects you: any INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE on a normal table fails with SQLSTATE 25006. The DEFERRABLE option has no effect unless the transaction is both SERIALIZABLE and READ ONLY.
Set a default level for a session, user or database

default_transaction_isolation can be set at every level PostgreSQL supports for settings. Its default is read committed and its context in pg_settings is user, so any user can change it for their own session without a reload.

content: SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
ALTER ROLE report_user SET default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read';
ALTER DATABASE isodemo SET default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read';
default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read' in /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf, then SELECT pg_reload_conf();

data.text: Here is the role-level setting tested end to end. As postgres, create a role, give it a default, and check what is stored:

data.caption: Per-role default (as postgres)

data.code:
rolname   |                     setconfig                     
-------------+---------------------------------------------------
 report_user | {"default_transaction_isolation=repeatable read"}
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: When report_user logs in, SHOW default_transaction_isolation returns repeatable read. A role setting wins over a database setting when both exist.
Role and database settings apply to new sessions only. To undo the change and drop the test role:

data.code:
ALTER ROLE report_user RESET default_transaction_isolation;
DROP ROLE report_user;
data.caption: Undo the per-role default

data.text: Think twice before changing the cluster-wide default. Code written for Read Committed often has no retry logic, and at Repeatable Read or Serializable it will start failing with SQLSTATE 40001 under load. Raise the level per transaction or per role, for code that is ready to retry.
Retrying serialization failures correctly

PostgreSQL does not retry failed transactions for you, because only the application knows which decisions it made from the data it read. Your code must catch the error and run the whole transaction again from BEGIN. The usual pattern looks like this:

data.caption: Retry loop (pseudocode for your application)

data.text: Points the documentation stresses:

items.content: Retry the complete transaction, including the reads and the logic that chooses values. Re-sending only the failed statement is wrong, because the values it uses came from an old snapshot.
Retry on SQLSTATE 40001 unconditionally. Deadlocks (40P01) are often worth retrying too. Be more careful with unique violations (23505), which can be a real, permanent error.
Under heavy contention a transaction may need several attempts, so cap the number of retries.
Do not trust data read inside a Serializable transaction until it has committed. A transaction that later fails may have read values that are not consistent.

data.text: Catching the error inside a PL/pgSQL function does not replace this: the error means the transaction must start again with a new snapshot, and with Serializable the failure can come at COMMIT, after your function has already returned.
Common mistakes
WARNING:  SET TRANSACTION can only be used in transaction blocks
You ran SET TRANSACTION without BEGIN. It has no effect; the next statement still runs in its own Read Committed transaction.

data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: use BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; or run SET TRANSACTION right after BEGIN.
ERROR:  SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL must be called before any query

data.caption: Output

data.text: The snapshot rules are fixed by the first query. Fix: roll back and set the level before the first SELECT. Watch out for drivers and ORMs that run a query of their own right after BEGIN.
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

Any error, including a serialization failure, aborts the transaction. Fix: run ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint) before sending more statements. In application code, make sure the error path always ends the transaction.
Expecting Read Uncommitted to be faster or to show dirty reads
It is the same as Read Committed in PostgreSQL. There is no speed gain and no dirty read.
Expecting sequences to roll back

Changes to sequences (and so to serial and identity columns) are visible to all transactions immediately and are not undone by ROLLBACK at any isolation level. Gaps in IDs after failed or retried transactions are normal.
Leaving transactions idle

A Repeatable Read or Serializable transaction left open holds its snapshot, keeps predicate locks and prevents VACUUM from removing dead rows. Keep transactions short and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as a safety net; see PostgreSQL DBA Part 10 for finding these sessions.
Performance tips and best practices

items.content: Keep Read Committed as the default. Write updates as expressions (balance = balance - 500) and use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE where you must read before writing.
Use Repeatable Read for reports and exports that run several queries and need one consistent view. Read-only Repeatable Read transactions never get serialization errors.

Use Serializable for business rules that span several rows or tables (like the on-call rule), where you would otherwise need table locks. Then you can drop the explicit locks and FOR UPDATE that Serializable makes unnecessary.
Declare transactions READ ONLY when they do not write. It lowers Serializable overhead and stops accidental writes.
Keep Serializable transactions small and the number of active connections under control, with a connection pool if needed.

A sequential scan always takes a relation-level predicate lock, which raises the failure rate. Good indexes for the WHERE clauses in serializable transactions help. If many page locks are combined into relation locks for lack of memory, the documentation suggests raising max_pred_locks_per_transaction, max_pred_locks_per_relation or max_pred_locks_per_page.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
Read Committed. It is controlled by default_transaction_isolation, whose default is read committed. The SQL standard's default is Serializable, but PostgreSQL ordinarily uses Read Committed.
Does PostgreSQL support Read Uncommitted?
You can request it and SHOW will report it, but it behaves exactly like Read Committed. PostgreSQL never returns uncommitted data.
What is the difference between Repeatable Read and Serializable in PostgreSQL?

Both read from one snapshot for the whole transaction and both raise SQLSTATE 40001 when they cannot continue safely. Serializable additionally tracks read/write dependencies between transactions and cancels one when the combined result could not come from any one-at-a-time order, which prevents write skew. That tracking adds some overhead but no extra blocking.
Does Serializable isolation lock tables in PostgreSQL?

No. Its SIReadLock predicate locks do not block other sessions and cannot cause deadlocks. The only case where a serializable transaction waits where Repeatable Read would not is SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE, which can wait at the start for a safe snapshot.
How do I fix "could not serialize access due to concurrent update"?

Roll back and run the whole transaction again. It is expected at Repeatable Read and Serializable whenever another transaction committed a change to a row you are trying to update or lock. If retries are not possible in your code, switch that transaction to Read Committed and use atomic updates or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE instead.
Summary

items.content: PostgreSQL has three real levels: Read Committed (default), Repeatable Read and Serializable. Read Uncommitted runs as Read Committed.
Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read and Serializable take one at the first statement of the transaction.
Avoid lost updates in Read Committed with UPDATE ... SET col = col - x or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
Repeatable Read raises "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" instead of losing an update.
Only Serializable prevents write skew; it reports "could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions", sometimes at COMMIT.
Set the level with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL ... or SET TRANSACTION before the first query; set defaults per role or database with ALTER ROLE / ALTER DATABASE.
Always retry the whole transaction on SQLSTATE 40001, and keep transactions short and READ ONLY where possible.

linkedin.post:
Two sessions both pass your "one doctor must stay on call" check. Both commit. Now nobody is on call.

Which PostgreSQL isolation level stops that? Here is what each one guarantees:

→ Read Committed (default): every statement takes a fresh snapshot, so two SELECTs in one transaction can disagree.
→ Read Uncommitted is accepted but runs as Read Committed. No dirty reads, ever.
→ Lost update: two sessions read 3000, the app writes 2500 and 2200, one payment vanishes. Fix it with SET balance = balance - 500 or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
→ Repeatable Read keeps one snapshot and fails with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" instead of losing a change.
→ Only Serializable stops write skew. The second COMMIT fails with SQLSTATE 40001, and the retry sees the new data.

The rule: at Repeatable Read or Serializable, your application must retry the whole transaction on 40001, not just the failed statement.

Which isolation level does your application run on, and does it have retry logic?

slides.title: Three real levels, not four
points: Read Uncommitted runs as Read Committed
No dirty reads at any level
Repeatable Read also blocks phantom reads

slides.title: Avoid the lost update
slides.code:
-- wrong: value computed in the app
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 2200
 WHERE account_id = 2;
-- right: let PostgreSQL compute it
UPDATE accounts
   SET balance = balance - 800
 WHERE account_id = 2;

slides.title: Repeatable Read: one snapshot
slides.body: All queries see the same data. If another session commits a change to a row you then update, you get: could not serialize access due to concurrent update (SQLSTATE 40001).

slides.title: Serializable stops write skew
points: Two doctors check the count, both go off call
Serializable fails one, often at COMMIT
